title: What Happens If You Disagree With Your Architect During Your Project
excerpt: Disagreements with your architect happen. Here's how to handle them productively and keep your renovation or new construction on track.
content:
You're three months into your kitchen remodel or home addition, and your architect presents designs that don't match what you envisioned. Your gut says something is off. Now what?

Disagreements between homeowners and architects are normal. They happen on projects across Westchester County, from renovations in Scarsdale to additions in Tarrytown to custom homes in Rye. The question isn't whether you'll disagree. It's how you handle it.

Listen First, Then Respond

Your first instinct might be to say no immediately. Resist that. Ask your architect why they made the choices they did. There's usually a reason behind the design.

Maybe the layout they proposed addresses a building code issue you didn't know existed. Maybe the material selection accounts for how your home's foundation sits. Maybe the window placement maximizes light in a way that wasn't obvious from your initial conversation. When working with a licensed architect in Westchester, NY, you're paying for expertise that goes beyond aesthetics.

Listen to the full explanation before deciding you disagree. You might find the design makes more sense than you thought.

Be Specific About What Bothers You

"I don't like it" doesn't give your architect anything to work with. "I don't like it" gets you nowhere on a second-story addition in Pelham or a bathroom renovation in Harrison.

Instead, pinpoint the problem. Is it the style? The color? The layout? The proportions? Is it practical or emotional? Are you worried about the cost, the timeline, or how it will look from the street?

The more specific you are, the faster your architect can adjust. They can't fix a vague complaint. They can absolutely work with a clear one.

Remember: Design and Execution Are Different

There's a real advantage to working with a general contractor in Westchester who is also your architect. Silvio M. Luca runs every project at House Architecture & Construction personally as both a licensed New York architect and licensed general contractor.

This matters when disagreements come up. Some architects design without fully considering how a home will actually be built. Some contractors build without understanding the design intent. When one person holds both licenses, holds both responsibilities, and runs the project, you eliminate finger-pointing.

If you disagree with a proposed design, you're discussing it with someone who knows exactly how it will be executed, what it will cost in real terms, and how it fits into your Westchester property's actual conditions. Whether your home renovation in Westchester, NY is a kitchen remodel in New Rochelle or a primary suite addition in Mamaroneck, that clarity matters.

Ask for Options, Not Arguments

If you genuinely disagree, ask your architect to present alternatives. Not one. Multiple directions.

This shifts the conversation from confrontation to collaboration. Instead of fighting over one design, you're exploring options together. You might see a third option you like even better, or you might realize the original choice was the strongest one after all.

Your architect should welcome this request. If they don't, that's a problem worth addressing early, whether you're working on historic restorations in Tarrytown or custom new construction in Ossining.
